texto:
Amazon Ads on September 29, 2026 published details of Review Requests, an advertising product that places review invitations in front of shoppers who recently bought an item, with an open beta in the United States scheduled for late October 2026 and eligibility limited to products with fewer than 1,000 total ratings and reviews.
In Short
Amazon is going to let sellers pay for ads that remind people who already bought their product to leave a star rating or a review. It matters most to brands with new products, because reviews help shoppers decide what to buy, and the ads stop once a product reaches 1,000 ratings and reviews. What changes is that collecting reviews, which used to depend on buyers remembering or on free tools, now has a paid option with its own budget and bids.
What Amazon published
The announcement sits on the Amazon Ads website under the label "launch announcement" and carries the title "Accelerate authentic reviews with Review Requests." Its central description is short. According to Amazon Ads, the product "reaches customers who recently purchased your product and invites them to submit a star rating or written review while they are shopping on Amazon."
The page illustrates the flow in three steps. A customer who recently purchased the product sees a Review Requests ad. That customer submits a rating "in one-click." The customer can then add an optional written review "with video or images." No screenshot on the page shows which Amazon surfaces carry the ad, and the text describes the placements only as "Amazon's highest-traffic pages."
Campaigns, according to Amazon Ads, are created and managed in Amazon Ads Agent "using the same bidding and budget controls" that advertisers use for other Amazon Ads campaigns. The page lists two access points: Amazon Ads Agent and the Amazon Ads Unified API. On the API side, Amazon Ads states that Review Requests campaigns "are an extension of the existing Unified Campaign Management API endpoints." Beyond that line, the page refers readers to their Amazon Ads account team.
Availability is a single marketplace for now. The page lists North America: United States, and adds that "additional marketplaces and Amazon properties are planned for future releases." No dates are attached to that expansion.
The 1,000-review ceiling
Eligibility has two layers. At the account level, Amazon Ads restricts the product to "registered sellers and vendors with an advertising console account in good standing and no active policy violations." At the product level, items qualify when they have fewer than 1,000 total ratings and reviews.
The check is not a one-time gate. According to Amazon Ads, eligibility is checked both when a campaign is created and while it runs, and Review Requests for a product "pause automatically once it reaches the ratings threshold of 1,000 reviews."
That sentence contains a small wording inconsistency. The eligibility rule counts "total ratings and reviews," while the pause rule describes "the ratings threshold of 1,000 reviews." On Amazon, a star rating without text and a written review are different things, and the distinction matters for a product with many ratings and few written reviews. Read together, the most likely meaning is a single combined count of ratings and reviews, but the page does not state it in one consistent way.
The cap tells sellers where Amazon sees the product's purpose. Review Requests is positioned as a tool for the early life of a listing, the stretch when a product has little social proof and conversion rates tend to suffer for it. Once a product crosses 1,000, the paid invitations stop and the product falls back on organic review volume.
The 3x claim and what sits behind it
Amazon Ads supports its case with one number. "Early test results show that products received three times as many ratings and reviews per week compared to before the test," the page states. A footnote identifies the source as "Internal Amazon data, Closed Beta, US, 3-21 June 2026."
That figure deserves to be read for what it is: company-supplied data from a closed beta lasting 19 days. The comparison is a before-and-after one, set against each product's own pre-test rate, rather than against a control group of similar products that did not run the ads. The page does not disclose how many products or advertisers took part, which categories were included, what the baseline weekly review counts were, how much was spent, or whether the share of positive and negative ratings shifted. A tripling from two reviews a week to six is a different commercial proposition from a tripling of 50 to 150, and the page gives no way to tell which applies. The window is also shorter than three full weeks, so a "per week" average rests on very few observations.
The page leans on a second argument that requires no data. "And because reviews live on your product detail page, the impact extends to every shopper who visits, not just those who saw your ad," according to Amazon Ads. That is a structural point: a review bought through an ad becomes a permanent asset on the listing, unlike a click that is spent once. It is also the reason measuring return on the product will be harder than for a standard Sponsored Products campaign, since much of the value would show up as conversion lift on traffic from other sources.
The page closes its pitch with a tagline: "Same authentic reviews customers already leave. Just more, and faster."
How the LinkedIn post describes it
The second document is a LinkedIn capture of a post by Will Haire, co-founder of the Amazon and Walmart agency BellaVix and host of the Selling on Giants podcast. The third document is a capture of Haire's LinkedIn profile, which lists 19,252 followers, a "Certified Amazon Advertising Partner" credential issued by Amazon in March 2022, and BellaVix as his company since March 2019. The profile establishes who wrote the commentary; it contains nothing about Review Requests.
Haire's post, headed "Amazon launches Review Requests to accelerate product reviews," is a summary of the Amazon Ads page with a link to it. The capture shows the post as six days old with 27 reactions, eight comments and one repost. The capture itself carries no date, so the exact publication day cannot be confirmed from the file; the link to the Amazon page means it was published after September 29.
Most of the summary tracks the source closely. Two details differ.
First, Haire writes that "In Amazon's closed beta, products using Review Requests received three times as many ratings and reviews per week as before the test." The Amazon page body says "early test results," and only the footnote names the closed beta. Haire's version is consistent with the footnote, though it drops the 3 to 21 June window that limits how much weight the number can carry.
Second, the eligibility line is shorter in the post. Haire describes eligible users as "Sellers and vendors with an advertising account in good standing." The Amazon page specifies registered sellers and vendors, an advertising console account, and "no active policy violations." The omitted condition is not trivial for sellers who have open policy issues on their accounts.
What the comments raise
The comment thread under Haire's post holds the more pointed reactions, and they cluster around cost and role.
Ravi Jaipaul, whose headline describes full-service Amazon management for founders, called it a "clean breakdown" and then set out the economics. "The number that decides whether to switch it on is not reviews per week, it is fully loaded cost per incremental review, because Amazon already gives you the free Request a Review button," Jaipaul wrote. "The ad is buying speed on top of a baseline you already get, so it only earns its cost on the reviews above that baseline." His comment is cut off in the capture at a reference to the "sub-1,000 cap."
The argument goes to the heart of the 3x claim. If a product already receives reviews through the free Request a Review button that Jaipaul refers to, a Seller Central tool, and through buyers who review unprompted, the relevant question is the incrementality of the paid invitation. A before-and-after comparison cannot separate the ad's effect from seasonality, a sales spike or other changes made during the test. Amazon has not published a cost-per-review figure, and the page does not describe the pricing model beyond saying campaigns use standard bidding and budget controls.
Jonny Golding, whose headline describes eCommerce growth systems, found the update "strange," writing that "reviews influence buyer trust and this pulls PPC into a part of the launch it never really owned." That observation points at an organisational change rather than a technical one: review generation has typically sat with listing management, customer experience or launch teams, and a paid version moves it into the advertising budget.
Two shorter comments were openly hostile. Raiyan Syed, who describes himself as an Amazon and marketplace growth leader, wrote: "Amazon finds unique way to loot sellers!" Bernard Nader, founder of PPC Maestro, wrote: "Pay for reviews? Who wants to do that."
Nader's framing compresses a distinction the Amazon page is careful about. According to Amazon Ads, the advertiser pays for an invitation shown to a verified purchaser, and the customer decides whether to respond and what to say. Nothing on the page suggests payment, discounts or other inducements to the reviewer. The word "authentic" appears in the product's title, and the page describes the result as the "same authentic reviews customers already leave." That framing matters in the United States, where the Federal Trade Commission finalized a rule on August 14, 2024 barring the purchase of positive or negative reviews. Paying a platform to ask buyers for feedback is a different act from paying for reviews, though the page does not explain whether reviews submitted through the ad will be labelled in any way on the product detail page.
Context: Amazon's review rules have been shifting
Review Requests arrives after a year in which Amazon changed how reviews and ratings work on its marketplace in several ways that affect smaller listings.
On July 29, 2025, Amazon told sellers that customers could submit seller feedback as star ratings alone from August 4, 2025, with the stated aim to "increase rating submissions." Sellers lost the ability to appeal star-only ratings through Feedback Manager.
On January 7, 2026, Amazon announced that review sharing between product variations would be restricted, with the change rolling out by category from February 12 to May 31, 2026. Only variations with minor, non-functional differences, such as colour, pattern or pack quantity, keep sharing reviews. In April 2026, Amazon added a review sharing eligibility check to Seller Assistant, its AI tool inside Seller Central.
The variation change is directly relevant to Review Requests. A child listing that once inherited hundreds or thousands of reviews from a parent product may now stand on its own count. Some of those listings will now sit below 1,000 and qualify for the paid invitations. The restriction created a pool of listings with thinner review counts; Review Requests offers a paid way to rebuild them.
Review integrity has also been a running seller complaint. In October 2026, PPC Land reported on a US Seller Forums thread about "malicious returns", in which sellers described uniform negative reviews arriving soon after deliveries and one best-selling product falling from 4.6 to 4.0 stars. The same article noted that Amazon said it blocked or removed more than 200 million suspected fake reviews in 2022. A product that solicits more ratings from verified buyers could dilute isolated hostile ratings on low-volume listings, but Amazon does not make that argument on the Review Requests page, and nothing in the documents addresses it.
Context: Ads Agent and the API
The choice of Amazon Ads Agent as the management surface follows a pattern. Amazon presented Ads Agent at its unBoxed conference on November 11, 2025, as an AI system that automates campaign management through natural language commands, initially focused on Amazon Marketing Cloud analytics and DSP campaign creation. The same week, Amazon unveiled a Campaign Manager combining the DSP and the Ads Console, alongside unified reporting. In February 2026, PPC Land reported that Amazon had opened its advertising APIs to AI agents through an MCP server.
Review Requests is described as an Ads Agent product from the start; the page does not mention a traditional campaign builder at all. For agencies that run campaigns through software, the more practical line is the API one: Review Requests extends the existing Unified Campaign Management API endpoints instead of requiring a new integration. The page does not say what new campaign types, targeting fields or metrics those endpoints will expose.
The commercial backdrop is large. Amazon reported advertising services revenue of $19.8 billion for the second quarter of 2026, up 26% from $15.7 billion a year earlier, with a trailing twelve-month total of $76.1 billion. A product that turns an activity sellers previously handled for free into a bidded placement, on Amazon's busiest pages, adds inventory to that business without requiring new traffic.
What the page leaves out
Several questions that will determine adoption are not answered in the source.
- Pricing model. The page does not say whether advertisers pay per impression, per click or per submitted rating.
- Placements. "Highest-traffic pages" is not defined; the page does not say whether the ads appear on the homepage, in order pages, in search results or on detail pages.
- Targeting window. "Recently purchased" is not quantified in days.
- Reporting. No metrics are named, so it is unclear whether advertisers will see ratings collected, reviews collected or the star distribution of responses.
- Labelling. The page does not say whether reviews generated through the ad are marked differently from other verified purchase reviews.
- Interaction with free tools. The page does not mention Amazon's existing free review request option or explain how the two interact for the same order.
The open beta in late October 2026 may answer some of these through the Ads Agent interface and API documentation. For now, the only performance figure available is Amazon's own, from 19 days of closed testing in June.
Timeline
- August 14, 2024: The FTC finalizes a rule barring the purchase of positive or negative consumer reviews
- July 29, 2025: Amazon announces star-only seller feedback, live from August 4, 2025
- November 11, 2025: Amazon presents Ads Agent at unBoxed, alongside Campaign Manager and unified reporting
- January 7, 2026: Amazon announces restrictions on review sharing between variations
- February 2, 2026: Amazon opens its advertising APIs to AI agents through an MCP server
- February 12 - May 31, 2026: Variation review sharing restrictions roll out by category
- June 3 - 21, 2026: Review Requests closed beta in the US, the source of Amazon's 3x weekly ratings and reviews figure
- July 30, 2026: Amazon reports Q2 2026 advertising revenue of $19.8 billion
- September 29, 2026: Amazon Ads publishes the Review Requests launch announcement
- After September 29, 2026: Will Haire, co-founder of BellaVix, summarises the announcement on LinkedIn; comments question cost per incremental review
- October 2026: PPC Land reports seller complaints about malicious returns and hostile reviews
- Late October 2026: Review Requests open beta scheduled to begin in the United States

Summary
Who: Amazon Ads, registered sellers and vendors in the United States with advertising console accounts in good standing, and commentators including Will Haire of BellaVix and Amazon agency operators in the LinkedIn comments.
What: Review Requests, a paid ad product that invites verified recent purchasers to leave a star rating or written review, managed in Amazon Ads Agent and through the Unified Campaign Management API, for products with fewer than 1,000 ratings and reviews. Amazon Ads says closed beta products received three times as many ratings and reviews per week as before the test, a company-supplied figure from a 19-day before-and-after comparison.
When: Announced on September 29, 2026; closed beta ran from June 3 to 21, 2026; US open beta scheduled for late October 2026.
Where: The United States only at launch, on what Amazon describes as its highest-traffic pages, with other marketplaces and Amazon properties planned without dates.
Why: Amazon Ads says new products need reviews to earn trust and many customers forget to leave one. For sellers, the product turns review collection into a bidded ad cost, which raises the cost-per-incremental-review question that Amazon's published data does not answer, particularly for listings left with thinner review counts after the 2026 variation sharing restrictions.
